nameStory: Rice cutgrass earned its memorable name from two distinctive features that anyone who meets this plant will remember! The "rice" part comes from its grain-like seeds that resemble wild rice, while "cutgrass" refers to the plant's notorious ability to slice through skin with its razor-sharp leaf edges. One careless brush against this grass will teach you why it's called cutgrass – those tiny teeth along the leaves are like nature's serrated knife!
description: Rice cutgrass is a tall, aggressive wetland grass that can grow 3-5 feet tall in boggy areas and along stream edges. It spreads by underground stems called rhizomes, often forming dense colonies that sway in the breeze like a green curtain. The plant produces loose, open flower clusters that branch out like delicate fingers, bearing small, flattened seeds. This native grass is both beautiful from a distance and treacherous up close – it's perfectly designed for wet feet and sharp defenses.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves up to 11 inches with wickedly sharp, minutely-toothed edges that feel like sandpaper and can easily cut skin. Run your finger along the edge very carefully – you'll feel the tiny teeth that give this grass its cutting power.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Loose, open clusters of tiny flowers on thread-like, wavy branches that emerge from the top of the plant. Each flower lacks the typical grass awns (bristles) and sits close to the branch like small, flattened beads.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through spreading underground stems, often creating large patches in wet areas. Individual stems grow 3-5 feet tall and tend to lean or arch over, especially when heavy with seeds.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened, rice-like grains with rough, bristly surfaces but no long awns. Seeds develop both in the visible flower clusters and hidden within leaf sheaths lower on the plant.

habitat: Rice cutgrass thrives in wet places throughout New England – look for it along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, and wet meadows. It prefers areas with rich, mucky soil that stays consistently moist or seasonally flooded. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants in both sunny and partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from rhizomes in late spring, growing rapidly in the warming, wet soil. Young leaves are slightly less sharp but still require careful handling.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and produce their delicate, branching flower clusters from mid to late summer. This is when the cutting ability of the leaves is at its peak.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and become more noticeable, while leaves begin to turn yellow-brown. The sharp leaf edges remain dangerous even as the plant starts to senesce.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems persist above ground, appearing as brittle, tan-colored stalks poking through snow. Seeds may still cling to dried flower clusters, providing food for wildlife.

funFact: Rice cutgrass produces two completely different types of flowers on the same plant – some showy ones you can see at the top, and secret "cleistogamous" flowers hidden inside the leaf sheaths that never open but fertilize themselves and produce seeds in complete privacy!
confusionNotes: Rice cutgrass might be confused with other tall wetland grasses, but the razor-sharp leaf edges are a dead giveaway – no other common wetland grass in New England will cut you quite like this one! If you can touch the leaf edges without getting sliced, it's probably something else.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its aggressive nature toward human skin, rice cutgrass is actually an important native plant used in wetland restoration projects and erosion control. The seeds were historically gathered by Native Americans as a food source, though harvesting required careful techniques to avoid the cutting leaves.
compareHints: Rice cutgrass differs from its relative white grass (also in the Leersia genus) by growing much taller and preferring wetter habitats – white grass is typically found in drier woods and fields. Both have the characteristic cutting leaf edges, but rice cutgrass has more open, branching flower clusters while white grass has more compact, narrow flower spikes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White grass differs from rice cutgrass in several key ways: its leaf sheaths are smooth rather than razor-sharp, its flower heads have single lower branches instead of multiple branches, and its spikelets overlap more tightly like roof shingles.
